newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil privatizations to boost debt issues in '97.
newsitem.headline: Brazil privatizations to boost debt issues in '97.

text.p: Brazilian firms eyeing stakes in government assets slated for privatization will tap external markets to finance part of their acquisitions, which should push foreign debt issuance to new heights in 1997, analysts said.

"This was a record year for debt issuance in Brazil and there should be even more next year due to the privatizations and the need to roll over old debt," said a head trader at a leading Brazilian investment bank.
Brazil issued about $16 billion in foreign debt between January and November of 1996, compared with $11.5 billion in all of 1995, according to the National Association of Investment Banks.
Analysts said the eurobond and euro commercial paper market would remain the most appealing markets for Brazilian firms due to more relaxed regulatory requirements than the U.S. "yankee" market.
Local and foreign investors are gearing up to bid for more than $15 billion in federal and state-owned assets bound for the auction block in 1997.

Federal mining firm Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, or CVRD, alone is estimated to be worth some $8 billion. Other attractive assets include Sao Paulo state's power companies and parts of the federal government's giant telephone monopoly concessions.

"Next year will be very interesting because we are going to see a lot of people raising money on international markets due to the privatizations," said Patrick Morin Jr., president of Chase Manhattan Corp's Brazilian unit.

Morin said Chase was advising a consortium made up of AT&T Corp's AT&T do Brasil, Globopar and other investors to bid for a concession to operate Band B cellular service in Brazil. The consortium may eventually tap some $1.0 billion in funds to invest in Band B service, he said.

An estimated $8.0 billion in federal and $3.0 billion in private investment was expected to be put into the telecommunications market alone in 1997. Traders expect much of the private investment to be financed through funds raised in the eurobond market.
"There is a great potential for the Band B cellular selloff, which will require a huge amount of financing for the concession and the equipment," said a eurobond trader who asked not to be named.

Other financing mechanisms available to investors include short-term bridge loans from banks, analysts said. This was the method preferred by some buyers of federal electricity utility Light Servicos de Electricidade SA, which was privatized in May for about $2.0 billion, and Rio de Janeiro state power firm Cerj, which sold for about $600,000 in November.

Brazil is Latin America's largest foreign debt issuer, accounting for some $12 billion of the region's total $42 billion in external paper issued between January and August of this year, analysts said.
